Taurus ships a small background service written in Rust, taurus-core. It serves system usage, compositor state, brightness, idle inhibition, screen time, launcher ranking and clipboard history to the shell. These used to be scripts and Python helpers that the shell ran on a timer or on every event. Now one long-running process answers them, so the shell no longer starts a process for each poll and no longer needs brightnessctl or python-jeepney.
Taurus ships its own blue light filter, taurus-gamma. It sets the color temperature, brightness, gamma and inversion of your displays on Wayland, with a day and night schedule that follows the sun.

Migrating from v1: All previous configuration will be backed up and unused. Configuration of compositor settings such as monitors, keybinds, and autostart is now up to you, as the project migrated from being dotfiles to being a shell.

Taurus ships skills: small folders that teach an AI coding agent (Claude Code, or any agent that reads ~/.agents/skills) how to customize, theme and troubleshoot this desktop. The idea is simple: the agent gets a stable, self-documenting command (taurus), a map of where everything lives, and a short list of rules, so it changes your setup the way you would. The skills are guidance, not magic. They work best when you run the agent in plan mode first and read what it proposes.

taurus agent skills install taurus agent skills status This links the Taurus skills into ~/.claude/skills (or $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/skills) and ~/.agents/skills. Links point to the installed copy, so updating Taurus updates the skills. A skill folder of your own with the same name is never replaced, and taurus agent skills uninstall removes only the links Taurus created. Then restart your agent and check that the skills appear (in Claude Code, type / and look for taurus). Taurus refuses to link from a cache folder or a git checkout, because those do not survive updates. Pass --force-path if you really want that.

Settings → AI clients (Mod+H) lists Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Gemini CLI. Tick the ones that are not installed yet and press Install selected: Taurus installs each from the repositories with pkexec pacman (Claude Code falls back to its own installer when your repositories do not carry it), then links the skills above for all of them. Clients that are already installed are only marked as such.

Installing Claude Code from this page, or linking its skills, also seeds ~/.claude/settings.json (or $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json) with a token-efficient setup: Setting Value Use model sonnet Main conversation: enough for everyday coding without paying for Opus on every message. advisorModel opus The server-side advisor, called only for the hard questions. CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL haiku Default for simple delegated tasks, which do not need a frontier model. Haiku is a default, not a rule: a model chosen for a single task, or a subagent with its own model field, still wins, so complex work can run on Sonnet or Opus. The built-in Explore and Plan subagents keep the main conversation's model. Taurus deliberately does not set CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE, which would force Haiku onto every subagent; if you set it yourself, your choice is kept. Your own settings win: Taurus only adds keys that are missing and never rewrites a value you chose. /model and /advisor inside Claude Code change the same file for new sessions. A settings.json that is not valid JSON is left untouched and reported as an error.

Skill Use it to taurus Change settings, themes, wallpaper, language and app theming; point it at the right compositor guide. taurus-make-theme Create a color preset of your own, or tweak how Taurus recolors another app. taurus-diagnose Find out why the shell, a popup or a companion service is not working, reading logs before changing anything. taurus-develop Work on the shell's source code in a git checkout: widgets, launcher tabs, settings, translations, tests.

Two commands give an agent the whole picture, and neither starts the shell: taurus commands --json lists every command with its usage and a risk level: read, change or disruptive. taurus info paths --json reports the install dir (and whether it is read-only), your settings, the shipped defaults, backups, state, logs and your own themes.

Configuration is files you own. The agent edits your settings and themes, never the install dir, which an update overwrites. Every write is backed up. taurus config copies settings.json to ~/.local/state/taurus/backups/ first. Undo the last change with taurus config restore latest, see your changes with taurus config diff, and reset one key with taurus config reset <key>. Disruptive commands need your approval: restarting the shell, locking, suspending, rebooting, powering off. No sudo, and no passwords. Configuring the shell never needs root. For the rare command that does, such as installing a package, the agent uses pkexec, so your system shows its own authentication dialog and the agent never sees a password. It tells you what the command does first. No changes to your compositor config unless you ask.
Launching an agent from the shell with a key, a launcher tab for prompts, and handing errors to an agent are not part of this first version.

Taurus ships its own small audio processor, taurus-audio. It replaces EasyEffects and depends only on PipeWire. The equalizer, balance, mono, channel swap, dynamic range modes and the dynamic EQ in the music popup all run on it. It creates a virtual output called Taurus, processes everything sent to it and plays the result on your real output device. The shell talks to it over a local socket, so changing a slider is instant.

taurusd start starts the engine, so it runs whenever the shell does. Your real device stays the default output. The engine moves each app's audio onto the Taurus output, processes it and plays it on the default device, just as EasyEffects did. The Taurus output appears in the volume popup next to your devices. Choosing a device in the volume popup moves the processed audio to that device. The volume keys and every app that asks for the default output see your real device. An app you move to another device yourself, for example in pavucontrol, stays there and skips the engine. Apps that pick their own device are left alone too. When the engine stops, apps go back to the default device. Settings survive a reboot. The engine keeps them in ~/.local/state/taurus/audio.state, and the music popup reads them back from there.

Voice chat apps skip the engine and play directly on your device, so their sound is not processed. Without this, the people in your call would hear their own voices when you share your screen with audio: the share leaves out the voice chat app, but the engine's processed mix contains its sound too, so it would be captured and sent back to them. These apps are skipped: Discord, including PTB and Canary Vesktop, Equibop, Legcord, ArmCord and WebCord Zoom Teams for Linux any app that marks its playback as call audio Everything these apps play skips the engine, including music and videos in them, so the equalizer and the dynamics modes do not apply to it. If you want an app processed anyway, move it to the Taurus output in pavucontrol. Each stream is checked only once, when it starts, so nothing switches devices in the middle of playback. Calls in Telegram and in a browser are still processed, because their call audio looks the same as the rest of their sound.

The Dynamic button on the equalizer page turns on an adaptive tonal balance. It listens to the last few seconds of audio and gently moves the balance toward the typical balance of commercial recordings, without changing loudness. It replaces the manual equalizer while it is on, so the sliders and presets are dimmed until you turn it off. The design and the research behind each number are described in the taurus-audio README.

The bar, widget, lock screen and music popup visualizers read their spectrum from taurus-audio visualizer, a port of cava's processing, so cava is no longer needed. The shell starts it only while music plays and a visualizer is on screen, and stops it shortly after the music stops. It runs separately from the engine, so the visualizer also works when the engine is off. The options are listed in the taurus-audio README.

The install script downloads the latest release for x86_64 or aarch64, checks it against the published checksums and installs it to /usr/local/bin. Prebuilt binaries need glibc 2.39 or newer. On other systems, such as Void Linux musl, the installer installs a compiler and the PipeWire development files and builds it from source. Running the installer again updates it. The Arch packages bundle a release, and the Nix flake builds it from source.

The first time the installer or the shell runs with the audio engine installed, Taurus undoes what it set up for EasyEffects. This runs once: stops the EasyEffects instance that the old equalizer started, the one running the live_eq preset, and ee-eq.service if it is running removes the live_eq preset that Taurus used to generate removes the systemctl --user enable --now easyeffects line from the autostart file Taurus installed for Hyprland, Niri, Sway or Mango, keeping a .pre-audio-engine.bak copy of each file it edits Anything you set up yourself stays as it is. EasyEffects stays installed, and your presets, services and autostart entries are not touched. An EasyEffects you started yourself keeps running. A line you moved or changed, and config files that are links, for example from Home Manager or a dotfiles manager, are left alone too. If EasyEffects is still running or set to start at login after this, Taurus tells you once: in the installer output, or as a notification when the shell starts. EasyEffects can interfere with the audio engine, so turn it off unless you use it for something else, such as microphone effects, which Taurus does not do. Depending on how you set it up, that means systemctl --user disable --now easyeffects, turning off its start-at-login option in EasyEffects, or removing services.easyeffects.enable from your Home Manager configuration.

Opens the settings as a panel inside the shell, like other popups. taurus settings: Open the settings. taurus settings <tab> [subtab]: Open directly on a tab, for example taurus settings theme. taurus settings toggle [tab]: Close the settings if they are open, otherwise open them. taurus settings close: Close the settings.
Runs standalone interface components in runner mode: taurus launch start [args...]: Launch first-time setup and onboarding wizard.

Sends raw IPC calls directly to the running shell: taurus ipc call <target> <method> [args...]: Forward call to target object. ipc call main handleCommand <cmd> <target> <arg>: Dispatch generic UI command. ipc call main forceReload: Force reload shell components. ipc call main clearNotifications: Purge all notification popups and history. ipc call lock activate: Trigger lock screen immediately. ipc call screenshotOverlay toggle [args...]: Toggle interactive screenshot overlay. ipc call floating toggle: Open the quick actions panel on the last used tab, or close it if it is open on any screen. Bind it to a key in your compositor, e.g. Hyprland: hl.bind(mainMod .. " + SHIFT + A", hl.dsp.exec_cmd("taurus ipc call floating toggle")). ipc call floating open / close: Open the panel on the screen under the cursor, or close it on every screen. Opened this way, it stays until closed, Escape is pressed, or the pointer enters and leaves it.

Exports your setup and imports someone else's. See Share your setup. taurus share export [-o FILE|-]: Write your changed settings, themes, scenes and layouts to a file (default taurus-setup.json, - for standard output). Personal and machine-specific data is left out and reported. taurus share import FILE: Preview what a file would change. Nothing is written. taurus share import FILE --apply: Apply it. Your settings are backed up first. --overwrite: Replace themes and scenes you already have. --layouts: Also replace your widget layouts (the old file is kept).

Checks what keeps the shell from running: the settings file, the daemon files, the shell process, its log and the companion services. See Self-healing. taurus doctor [--json]: Report. It only reads. Exit status 0 means all good, 1 warnings, 2 failures. taurus doctor --fix: Also apply the safe repairs: restore a settings.json that does not parse, remove stale pid files, undo a dangling scene.

Switches scenes: taurus scene list [--json]: List the scenes. The active one is marked. taurus scene show <name>: Print a scene. taurus scene apply <name>: Apply a scene by hand. Automatic switching leaves it alone. taurus scene off: Undo the active scene. Values you changed meanwhile are kept. taurus scene status [--json]: Show the active scene and whether automatic switching is on. taurus scene save <name> [fields...]: Save the current values as a scene of your own. taurus scene delete <name>: Delete a scene of your own. taurus scene auto <on|off|status>: Turn automatic switching (by focused app and time) on or off.

Lists every command with its usage and a risk level, so a person or an AI agent can discover the whole CLI: taurus commands: Print a table. taurus commands --json: Print the registry as JSON. The risk levels are read (only reads state), change (changes settings or UI state, reversible) and disruptive (interrupts the session, locks or powers off the machine, or restarts the shell). commands never starts the shell.

Manages the AI agent skills: taurus agent skills install [--force-path]: Link the Taurus skills into ~/.claude/skills (or $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/skills) and ~/.agents/skills, plus the skills folder of Codex (~/.codex/skills), Gemini CLI (~/.gemini/skills) and OpenCode (~/.config/opencode/skills) when they are installed. A skill folder of your own with the same name is never replaced. It refuses to link from a cache folder or a git checkout unless you pass --force-path. taurus agent skills uninstall: Remove only the links Taurus created. taurus agent skills status [--json]: Show what is linked.
Stops the daemon and terminates all background shell workers (taurus-core screentime track, quickshell, taurusd).
Stops the daemon and starts it again.

Reads and writes settings.json. Keys use dots to reach nested values and changes apply live: taurus config get <key> [fallback]: Print a setting. taurus config set <key> <value>: Set a setting. Values are parsed as JSON and fall back to plain strings. taurus config dump: Print the whole settings file. taurus config path: Print the settings file path. taurus config edit: Open the settings file in $VISUAL or $EDITOR. taurus config reset <key>: Restore a key to the value shipped with the install, or remove it when there is no shipped default. taurus config diff: Show what you changed compared with the shipped defaults. taurus config backup: Back up the settings now. taurus config backups: List the backups, newest first. taurus config restore [file|latest]: Restore a backup. It backs up the current file first. Every write made through taurus (config set, config reset, set ...) first copies the settings file to ~/.local/state/taurus/backups/ and keeps the newest 20. config set warns, without blocking, when a key is not in the shipped defaults, which usually means a typo.

Prints the current state of a group as JSON. Add a key to print just that value, for example taurus info dock autohide. Lists print one item per line: taurus info notifications [dnd]: Do not disturb. taurus info idle [key]: Idle system state: whether idle is active, caffeine and its seconds remaining (0 when it has no time limit), app and media inhibitors, and each action's timeout and status. taurus info dock [enabled|autohide]: Dock visibility and autohide. taurus info sfx [mute]: Interface sound effects muted. taurus info theme [preset|matugen|apps|presets]: Active preset, wallpaper-derived colors, apps that follow the palette and the available presets (bundled and your own). taurus info lang [current|available]: Active language code and available codes. taurus info wallpaper [screen]: Current wallpaper path. taurus info monitors [--json]: Active outputs, with width, height and refresh rate as JSON. taurus info updates [--json]: Installed version compared with the latest release. taurus info paths [--json]: Where things are: install dir (and whether it is read-only), settings, shipped defaults, backups, state, cache, logs, your own themes and the bundled ones.

Controls color temperature and the day/night schedule through taurus-gamma, which it starts when needed. Taurus stops it on exit, and the compositor then restores normal colors. taurus gamma set <temperature> [output] [mode] [latitude] [longitude]: Set temperature (1000-10000K) manually (mode=manual), or use it as the night temperature of the solar schedule (mode=auto). Without coordinates, or with 0 0, the schedule fades to night at 19:00 and to day at 06:30. Without an output, every output is changed. taurus gamma reset [output]: Reset color temperature to 6500K daylight neutral and turn the schedule off. taurus gamma status [output]: Print status (running or stopped). taurus gamma start: Start taurus-gamma if it is not running. taurus gamma stop: Stop taurus-gamma. taurus gamma --verbose (-v): Print verbose output with current Kelvin, brightness and schedule state.

Reloads shell: taurus reload: Force reload QuickShell desktop elements without restarting the daemon.
Terminates desktop session: taurus exit: Cleanly terminate graphical session and exit active compositor.
taurus suspend: Lock the screen and suspend the system. taurus hibernate: Hibernate the system. taurus reboot: Reboot the system. taurus poweroff: Power off the system.

taurusd is the background service daemon for the desktop shell.
-v, --verbose: Enable verbose logging output. -V, --version: Print installed version and exit. -h, --help: Show usage help and exit.
taurusd start: Start the desktop shell and background services, including the audio engine (default command).
taurusd stop: Stop the running daemon and all background shell processes (taurus-core screentime track, quickshell).
taurusd status: Check whether the daemon is currently running (exit code 0 if running, 1 if stopped).

Taurus can recolor other apps with the same palette as the shell, whether it comes from the wallpaper (Matugen) or from a preset. Open Settings → Theme → App theming. The page lists the apps that are currently themed. Add another one from Add app, or remove one with the delete button on its tile. Add app only offers apps that are installed. Nothing is installed for you, and an app that is switched on but not installed is skipped. On by default: Bash, Kitty, Cava, GTK and Qt. Everything else is opt-in.

Every time the colors change, Taurus renders each enabled app's template with matugen into a separate theme file, such as ~/.config/kitty/themes/taurus.conf. It then adds a single include line to the app's own config so the app loads that file. Your config files are never overwritten. The lines Taurus adds are wrapped in markers: # >>> taurus theme >>> include themes/taurus.conf # <<< taurus theme <<< If one of your existing lines would override the theme (for example another theme = line), it is commented out as # taurus-disabled: .... When you switch an app off, Taurus removes its block, restores the lines it commented out, deletes the generated theme file and puts back any setting values it changed. A config file it had to create is removed again if nothing else was added to it. When a config can't be edited safely, for example because it is a read-only file managed by Home Manager or its structure is unusual, nothing is changed. A warning button appears on the app's tile. Click it to see what went wrong and the exact line to add yourself, with buttons to copy it and to open the folder. Apps are only reloaded when their colors actually changed. A broken template only affects its own app, never the shell or other apps.

Press the edit button on an app's tile. Its files are copied to ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/taurus/matugen/apps/<app>/ and the folder opens. The folder button at the top of the page opens the parent folder. The template files use matugen syntax, such as {{colors.primary.default.hex}}, {{colors.surface.default.hex_stripped}} or {{mode}}. They are rendered again on every color change. app.json describes where the theme file goes and which line is added to the app's config. It usually doesn't need changes. The reset button restores the built-in version. Your copy is kept in ~/.local/state/taurus/matugen/backup/. Only built-in apps can be customized this way. Folders with other names are ignored.
taurus info theme apps taurus set theme app <id> [on|off|toggle]

Configuration is stored in ~/.config/hypr. The main file is hyprland.lua, which loads modules from the config/ directory: variables.lua - modifier keys and default applications env.lua - environment variables autostart.lua - startup processes monitors.lua - display and resolution setup settings.lua - window decorations, blur, animations, and input keybinds.lua - keybindings for compositor actions and shell controls

The shell daemon and clipboard history are launched from config/autostart.lua: hl.on("hyprland.start", function() hl.exec_cmd("wl-paste --type text --watch cliphist store") hl.exec_cmd("wl-paste --type image --watch cliphist store") hl.exec_cmd("taurusd start") end) taurusd start also starts the audio engine.

Shell overlays and controls are bound in config/keybinds.lua using taurus msg toggle <module>: launcher - application launcher system - system control panel clipboard - clipboard history music - media player wallpaper - wallpaper selector calendar - calendar popout network - wi-fi and network connections volume - audio output and input slider settings - cheat sheet for keybindings Workspace switching is routed through the shell to update bar indicators: for i = 1, 10 do hl.bind("SUPER + " .. (i % 10), hl.dsp.exec_cmd("taurus msg workspace " .. i)) hl.bind("SUPER + SHIFT + " .. (i % 10), hl.dsp.exec_cmd("taurus msg workspace " .. i .. " move")) end Quick utility actions: Lock screen: taurus lock Reload shell: taurus reload Bar autohide: taurus msg bar autohide Screenshots: taurus screenshot (add --edit, --full, or --full --edit) Brightness: taurus brightness lower and taurus brightness raise Volume: taurus volume lower, taurus volume raise, and taurus volume mute-toggle

Mouse wheel (with SUPER): the main wheel switches workspaces (e+1 / e-1, no wrap) and the thumb wheel (for example on an MX Master) moves focus left and right. The active and inactive border colors follow the theme: Taurus applies them with hyprctl on every color change, so a Hyprland reload resets them until the next change.

Configuration is stored in ~/.config/mango. The main file is config.conf, which includes modular files from config/: input - keyboard layout and touchpad settings layout - tag count, window borders, and gaps autostart - startup processes keybinds - keybindings for compositor actions and shell controls The bundled files use the option names of Mango 0.18. Older releases used different names (for example gappih and exec-once), so update to 0.18 or later. Validate a config without starting the compositor using mango -c ~/.config/mango/config.conf -p.

The shell daemon and clipboard history are launched from config/autostart.conf: exec_once=wl-paste --type text --watch cliphist store exec_once=wl-paste --type image --watch cliphist store exec_once=taurusd start taurusd start also starts the audio engine.

Shell overlays and controls are bound in config/keybinds.conf using spawn,taurus msg toggle <module>, with the same keys as the other compositors: bind=SUPER,D,spawn,taurus msg toggle launcher bind=SUPER,B,spawn,taurus msg toggle system Tag switching is routed through the shell to update bar indicators. Mango has nine tags by default (tag_num): bind=SUPER,1,spawn,taurus msg workspace 1 bind=SUPER+SHIFT,1,spawn,taurus msg workspace 1 move
Mango uses tags instead of workspaces. The bar shows the lowest active tag of each monitor as the current workspace and marks tags that hold windows as occupied.

The UI scale setting is hidden because output scale cannot be changed at runtime. Set it with monitor_rule in the config. The output toggle in display settings puts the monitor to sleep instead of removing it.

Mouse wheel (with SUPER, axisbind): the main wheel switches tags and the thumb wheel (for example on an MX Master) moves focus left and right. focuscolor and bordercolor follow the theme: Taurus rewrites config/focus-colors.conf on every color change and reloads the config.

Configuration is stored in ~/.config/niri. The main file is config.kdl, which includes files from the config/ directory: env.kdl - environment variables input.kdl - keyboard layout, touchpad, and mouse settings output.kdl - display and resolution setup layout.kdl - gaps, column width, and border settings autostart.kdl - startup processes keybinds.kdl - keybindings for compositor actions and shell controls focus-colors.kdl - focus ring colors, generated by Taurus from the current theme (do not edit)

The shell daemon and clipboard history are launched from config/autostart.kdl: spawn-at-startup "bash" "-c" "wl-paste --type text --watch cliphist store" spawn-at-startup "bash" "-c" "wl-paste --type image --watch cliphist store" spawn-at-startup "taurusd" "start" taurusd start also starts the audio engine.

Shell overlays and controls are bound in config/keybinds.kdl using spawn "taurus" "msg" "toggle" "<module>": launcher - application launcher (Mod+D) system - system control panel (Mod+B) clipboard - clipboard history (Mod+C) music - media player (Mod+M) wallpaper - wallpaper selector (Mod+W) calendar - calendar popout (Mod+S) network - network connections (Mod+N) volume - audio popout (Mod+V) settings - cheat sheet for keybindings (Mod+H) Workspace switching is routed through the shell to update bar indicators: Mod+1 { spawn "taurus" "msg" "workspace" "1"; } Mod+2 { spawn "taurus" "msg" "workspace" "2"; } // ... Mod+Shift+1 { spawn "taurus" "msg" "workspace" "1" "move"; } Mouse wheel (with Mod): the main wheel switches workspaces and the thumb wheel (for example on an MX Master) moves between columns. Both stop at the edges. Remove Mod+ from those lines in keybinds.kdl to use the wheel alone. The focus ring follows the theme: every time Matugen or a preset changes the colors, Taurus rewrites config/focus-colors.kdl (active ring = primary color) and niri reloads it. Older configs get the include "config/focus-colors.kdl" line added after layout.kdl automatically. Quick utility actions: Lock screen: Mod+L { spawn "taurus" "lock"; } Reload shell: Mod+R { spawn "taurus" "reload"; } Bar autohide: Mod+A { spawn "taurus" "msg" "bar" "autohide"; } Screenshots: Print { spawn "taurus" "screenshot"; } (add --edit or --full) Brightness: XF86MonBrightnessDown and XF86MonBrightnessUp Volume: XF86AudioLowerVolume, XF86AudioRaiseVolume, and XF86AudioMute

Settings → Display → General shows, for each screen, a resolution and a refresh rate list built from the modes the screen reports, a Variable refresh rate (VRR) switch (only when the screen supports it) and a rotation list. A change is applied at once, then Taurus asks you to keep it. If you do not confirm within 15 seconds (for example because the screen went black), it goes back to what it was. Keep saves the screen's mode, scale, rotation and VRR in ~/.config/niri/config/output.kdl, between two comment lines that mark the block as Taurus's. If that file already has an output "NAME" block of your own, Taurus does not write a second one: it tells you to edit yours by hand. VRR has three modes: Off, Always on (variable-refresh-rate) and Only in games (variable-refresh-rate on-demand=true). In the games mode the screen only uses VRR while a game window is shown, so Taurus adds a window-rule to output.kdl, between two comment lines, that matches Steam games (steam_app_*) and gamescope. Add your own match lines inside that block for other launchers; Taurus never rewrites the block once it exists.
documents.s: Screen resolution, refresh rate, VRR and rotation

documents.t: Configuration is stored in ~/.config/sway. The main file is config, which includes modular files from configDir/: variables - modifier keys and default applications input - keyboard and touchpad settings output - display and monitor configurations layout - window borders and gaps autostart - startup processes window-rules - floating window rules and assignments keybinds - keybindings for compositor actions and shell controls

The shell daemon and clipboard history are launched from configDir/autostart: exec wl-paste --type text --watch cliphist store exec wl-paste --type image --watch cliphist store exec taurusd start taurusd start also starts the audio engine.

Shell overlays and controls are bound in configDir/keybinds using exec taurus msg toggle <module>: launcher - application launcher ($mod+D) system - system control panel ($mod+B) clipboard - clipboard history ($mod+C) music - media player ($mod+M) wallpaper - wallpaper selector ($mod+W) calendar - calendar popout ($mod+S) network - network connections ($mod+N) volume - audio popout ($mod+V) settings - cheat sheet for keybindings ($mod+H) Workspace switching is routed through the shell to update bar indicators: bindsym $mod+1 exec taurus msg workspace 1 bindsym $mod+Shift+1 exec taurus msg workspace 1 move # ... up to workspace 10 ($mod+0) Quick utility actions: Lock screen: $mod+L exec taurus lock Reload shell: $mod+R exec taurus reload Bar autohide: $mod+A exec taurus msg bar autohide Screenshots: Print exec taurus screenshot (add --edit or --full) Brightness: XF86MonBrightnessDown and XF86MonBrightnessUp Volume: XF86AudioLowerVolume, XF86AudioRaiseVolume, and XF86AudioMute

Mouse wheel (with $mod): the main wheel switches workspaces and the thumb wheel (for example on an MX Master) moves focus left and right. Sway wraps around at the ends. The focused border follows the theme: Taurus applies client.focused / client.unfocused at runtime on every color change, so a swaymsg reload resets them until the next change.

Configuration is stored in ~/.config/umbriel. The main file is config.toml, which includes modular files from config/: input - keyboard layout and touchpad settings layout - window gaps and borders autostart - startup processes keybinds - keybindings for compositor actions and shell controls The bundled files use the current action syntax, where an action and its arguments are separated by spaces (workspace-switch 3, spawn kitty). Older Umbriel builds used a colon (spawn:kitty) and reject these files, so use a current build. Validate a config without starting the compositor using umbriel config validate -c ~/.config/umbriel/config.toml. NixOS Nixpkgs currently ships an older snapshot of Umbriel that still uses the colon syntax and rejects these files. Use the upstream flake, which provides current builds. Add inputs.umbriel.url = "github:noctalia-dev/umbriel";, then import its module and enable it: { inputs, ... }: { imports = [ inputs.umbriel.nixosModules.default ]; programs.umbriel.enable = true; }

The shell daemon and clipboard history are launched from config/autostart.toml: [general] show_cheatsheet = false autostart = [ "wl-paste --type text --watch cliphist store", "wl-paste --type image --watch cliphist store", "taurusd start", ] Umbriel runs each entry through /bin/sh. taurusd start also starts the audio engine.

Umbriel's default binds live in its packaged config.toml, which it only loads when no user configuration exists, so config/keybinds.toml lists every bind. The packaged Mod bind that opens the Noctalia launcher is not included. Mod is the Super key. Shell overlays and controls use spawn taurus msg toggle <module>, with the same keys as the other compositors: [keybinds] "Mod+D" = { action = "spawn taurus msg toggle launcher", repeat = false } "Mod+B" = { action = "spawn taurus msg toggle system", repeat = false } Window and workspace controls use native Umbriel actions: Key Action Mod+Return, Mod+F, Mod+E Open kitty, Firefox and Ski Mod+Q window-close Mod+Shift+F window-toggle-floating Mod+BackSpace scratchpad-toggle Mod+Left, Mod+Right window-focus-left, window-focus-right Mod+Up, Mod+Down workspace-previous, workspace-next Mod+Ctrl+Left, Mod+Ctrl+Right column-move-left, column-move-right Mod+Ctrl+Up, Mod+Ctrl+Down window-move-to-workspace-previous, window-move-to-workspace-next Mod+Shift+Left, Mod+Shift+Right window-modify-primary-extent by -0.05 and +0.05 Mod+Shift+Up, Mod+Shift+Down window-modify-secondary-extent by -0.05 and +0.05 Mod+1 to Mod+9 workspace-switch <n> Mod+Shift+1 to Mod+Shift+9 window-move-to-workspace <n> Moving a window to a workspace follows it there. Volume and brightness keys repeat while held, while launchers and toggles do not. The bind that quits the session is not set. Add "Mod+Escape" = "session-quit" to config/keybinds.toml if you want one.

Workspaces belong to each output and are dynamic: Umbriel keeps one empty workspace at the end and removes empty ones when you leave them, so there is no fixed count. To use a fixed set instead, set workspaces on an output in your own config.toml, as described in the Umbriel documentation.
New windows open in Umbriel's default scrolling layout. The bundled config only sets a 4 px gap and removes window borders. Change the layout mode with layout.mode in config/layout.toml.

Mouse wheel (with Mod): Mod+WheelUp / Mod+WheelDown switch workspaces and Mod+WheelLeft / Mod+WheelRight (the thumb wheel on an MX Master) move focus, all with a 150 ms cooldown. The bundled config has no window borders, so there is no border color to sync.
Taurus checks itself and repairs the few things that can be repaired safely. Nothing here needs you to do anything; this page explains what happens and how to check it by hand.

taurus doctor # report: settings, daemon files, shell, log, services taurus doctor --json taurus doctor --fix # also apply the safe repairs below taurus doctor exits with 0 when all is well, 1 for warnings and 2 for failures. Without --fix it only reads.

Problem Repair settings.json is not valid JSON Restores the last known good copy, or the newest backup that parses. The broken file is kept next to it as settings.broken.<time>.json. Stale daemon pid or lock files Removes them. An active scene whose file is gone Undoes the scene. It never restores your settings because of a QML error in the log: that is a bug in the code, and restoring would throw away valid changes of yours. It reports those errors and leaves the decision to you.
documents.s: What it repairs, and what it never does

documents.t: The daemon checks settings.json before it launches the shell. A file that does not parse is the commonest reason the shell never comes up, and it is repaired from the last known good copy first. A copy becomes the last known good once the settings have been untouched for a minute, the shell is running and its log shows no new errors. It is stored in ~/.local/state/taurus/last-good/, apart from the backups.

The daemon restarts the shell once. It does not restart when the shell exits cleanly, when you stop it with taurus kill, or when your session has ended (it waits a moment and checks again, so a logout is not mistaken for a crash). Anything that kills the shell from outside, such as pkill quickshell, counts as a crash and gets one restart: use taurus kill to stop the shell on purpose. The crashed shell's leftover helper processes are ended before the restart. If a restarted shell dies again within 20 seconds, or the shell has been restarted twice in ten minutes, the daemon stops instead of looping. Because the shell is also the notification server, nothing can be shown while it is down. Once it is running again, a notification tells you what happened, with a Diagnose button. The button opens a terminal with the taurus doctor report and, if Claude Code is installed, offers to investigate with the taurus-diagnose skill. It asks before doing anything. If the shell could not be restarted, the same notification appears the next time it starts.

A scene is a named bundle of settings that switch together: do not disturb, dock and bar autohide, interface sounds, caffeine, the theme and the screen warmth. Switch one by hand, or let Taurus switch it for you when a game is focused or the evening starts. taurus scene list taurus scene apply gaming taurus scene off Three scenes ship with Taurus: work (do not disturb, quiet), gaming (no interruptions, autohide, caffeine) and night (warm screen, quiet).

A scene is a JSON file with a fixed set of fields. There are no commands in it, so a scene someone shares with you can never run anything. Field What it sets dnd Do not disturb. dock_autohide, bar_autohide Hide the dock or the bar until the pointer arrives. mute_sfx Interface sound effects. caffeine Keep the screen awake. theme A theme preset by name, or matugen to follow the wallpaper. gamma_temperature Screen warmth in kelvin, from 1000 to 10000. Needs taurus-gamma. Setting a temperature pauses the blue light filter's day and night schedule while the scene is active. Turning the scene off brings the schedule back with your own day and night temperatures, or your manual temperature if you had one. Applying a scene remembers what each field was. Turning it off puts a field back only if it still holds what the scene wrote: a value you changed in the meantime is kept. Switching from one scene to another restores the first before applying the second, so nothing leaks from one to the next. Scene changes are not part of the settings backups, so switching scenes automatically never pushes your own backups out. Use taurus scene off to undo a scene, and taurus config restore latest to undo your own change.
documents.s: What a scene changes, and how it undoes it

documents.t: Automatic switching is off until you turn it on: taurus scene auto on A scene can name the windows and the hours that activate it: { "name": "gaming", "dnd": true, "dock_autohide": true, "triggers": { "apps": ["steam_app_*", "gamescope", "lutris"], "time": {"from": "22:00", "to": "07:00"} } } apps are window classes, with * as a wildcard. A matching focused window beats a matching time. time is a window of the day and may cross midnight, as in 22:00 to 07:00. The shell's own windows, such as the launcher, never end a scene. A scene you applied by hand is never overridden by the automatic ones, until you turn it off.

Put your files in ~/.config/taurus/scenes/<name>.json. A scene of yours with the same name as a bundled one replaces it. taurus scene save focus dnd mute_sfx theme # capture the current values taurus scene show focus taurus scene delete focus taurus scene list shows an invalid scene with the reason, and Taurus refuses to apply it.

Export what makes your Taurus yours into one file, send it to someone, and let them preview and import it. taurus share export -o my-setup.json taurus share import their-setup.json # preview only, nothing changes taurus share import their-setup.json --apply # apply it

The settings you changed from the defaults, not the whole settings file. Your own themes (~/.local/state/taurus/themes/) and scenes (~/.config/taurus/scenes/). Your widget layouts: position, size, type and variant of each widget.

Export leaves out anything personal or specific to your machine, and tells you exactly what it skipped: Your avatar, location, anything that looks like a token, key, password or e-mail, and any value that holds a file path. Your monitors, the apps pinned in your dock, the notification sound file, do not disturb and other runtime state. Text, images and lists inside widgets (notes, GitHub names, photos). Only position, size and simple numbers and switches stay. Wallpapers, and the Matugen overrides that edit other apps' config files. Read the file before you send it: it is plain JSON.

A setup file is untrusted, so importing is careful by design. Preview first. taurus share import FILE only shows what would change, and what it ignored and why. Add --apply to apply it. A backup of your settings is made first, so taurus config restore latest undoes it. Only real options. A setting is applied only if it exists in the shipped defaults with the same type, and is small plain data. Unknown or wrongly typed values are ignored, not fatal. Themes must have all the color roles as #rrggbb. A theme named like a bundled one is renamed with -shared, so it never hides it. One you already have is skipped unless you pass --overwrite. Scenes go through the same closed schema as your own: they contain no commands, so a shared scene cannot run anything. Layouts replace yours, so they are opt-in: add --layouts. Your current layout is kept as layout.json.bak, and only monitors with the same name as yours are touched. Files larger than 1 MB, or not made by taurus share, are refused.
documents.s: Importing a file from someone else

documents.t: Taurus ships a small background service written in Rust, taurus-core. It serves system usage, compositor state, brightness, idle inhibition, screen time, launcher ranking and clipboard history to the shell. These used to be scripts and Python helpers that the shell ran on a timer or on every event. Now one long-running process answers them, so the shell no longer starts a process for each poll and no longer needs brightnessctl or python-jeepney. It talks to the shell over the D-Bus session bus, works on any compositor and links only glibc. The same binary is its command line client, and every command prints JSON, one object or array per line.

The daemon starts the first time anything asks for it, and every command except quit starts it when it is not running. watch starts it again if it goes away. taurusd start runs taurus-core screentime track for the digital wellbeing tab, and taurusd stop ends it. The daemon can outlive a login. taurus-core quit stops it.

The daemon samples a feed only while a client holds a lease on it. A lease ends when the client exits or leaves the bus, so closing a popup that shows CPU usage stops the sampling. When several clients watch the same feed, it samples at the shortest interval any of them asked for.

Command Used for sysinfo, watch sysinfo [--interval S] CPU, memory, temperature, network and disk usage in the system monitor watch locks Caps Lock and Num Lock in the on-screen display watch compositor Workspaces, windows and keyboard layout on Sway, Niri, Mango and Umbriel watch brightness, brightness get|set|raise|lower|backend Brightness sliders, keys and the on-screen display watch idle MARKER Idle inhibition and the sleep lock screentime track, screentime stats [DATE] Counting and reading screen time launcher rank, launcher log NAME, launcher files QUERY App ranking, launch counts and file search in the launcher monitors Monitor lists in the wallpaper picker, the bar's workspace settings and taurus info monitors system can-hibernate, system fingerprint Whether the system panel offers hibernate, and whether fingerprint unlock is set up clipboard list|pin|delete|wipe The clipboard history taurus-core --help lists every command.
sysinfo reads /proc and /sys and prints CPU, memory, temperature, network and disk values as one JSON object.

Caps Lock and Num Lock follow the keyboards' LED events when /dev/input can be read, for example as a member of the input group, and nothing runs between changes. Otherwise the LEDs in /sys/class/leds are polled every 250 ms while someone watches, because the kernel sends no change events there. On Hyprland every change is checked against Hyprland's main keyboard, which ignores LED flicker from other keyboards.

The compositor feed speaks each compositor's own socket: Sway's i3-ipc, Niri's JSON socket, Mango's IPC socket and Umbriel's JSON socket at $UMBRIEL_SOCKET, so following them costs no processes. Every watcher passes the variables that locate its compositor, because the daemon may outlive a login. Hyprland is read natively by the shell. Of Hyprland, the daemon follows only the focused window, which screen time needs.

monitors prints the outputs in use with their size and refresh rate, asked over the same sockets and Hyprland's. On other Wayland compositors it reads wl_output, and without a compositor it lists the connectors the kernel reports connected.

Brightness drives the first backlight in /sys/class/backlight. When its file is not writable, it goes through logind, as brightnessctl does. Without a backlight it drives the first DDC/CI display through ddcutil, which then needs to be installed. brightness backend prints backlight, ddc or none, and brightness get prints -1 when there is nothing to read.

While watch idle runs, the daemon serves org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver, so video players and other apps can keep the screen awake. With the sleep lock on, it also holds a logind sleep delay inhibitor for up to 4 seconds, so the system waits for the lock screen to appear before it suspends. The lock screen signals this by creating the marker file passed to the command.

Screen time counts the focused app once a second into the shell's database, per day, hour, quarter hour and minute. It follows the compositor feed for the focus, and notifies you when a daily limit from the shell's settings is reached. The statistics in the digital wellbeing tab come from screentime stats. A database from the earlier Python daemon, in ~/.local/share/focustime, is moved to the shell's state directory on first use.

launcher rank scores apps from screen time and launches, both decaying by half a week at a time. launcher log counts a launch, and launcher files searches files, or completes the path when the query is one.
The clipboard commands read the history from cliphist, which must be installed. Decoded images and pins are kept in the directory passed with --cache-dir, by default $XDG_CACHE_HOME/taurus/clipboard.

The daemon owns org.taurus.Core on the session bus, with one object per feed: Object Interface / org.taurus.Core /sysinfo org.taurus.Core.SysInfo /locks org.taurus.Core.Locks /compositor org.taurus.Core.Compositor /brightness org.taurus.Core.Brightness /idle org.taurus.Core.Idle /screentime org.taurus.Core.ScreenTime /clipboard org.taurus.Core.Clipboard Properties signal PropertiesChanged. You can query it by hand: busctl --user call org.taurus.Core /sysinfo org.taurus.Core.SysInfo Subscribe u 1000 busctl --user get-property org.taurus.Core /sysinfo org.taurus.Core.SysInfo Cpu The full list of members is in the taurus-core README.

The install script downloads the latest release for x86_64, checks it against the published checksums and installs it to /usr/local/bin. On other architectures it prints a warning and leaves the shell without the core services, so build it from source there. Running the installer again updates it, and it does nothing when the installed version is already the latest. The Arch packages bundle a release, and the Nix flake builds it from source.
taurus-core --version taurus-core sysinfo The second command should print one JSON object with your CPU, memory, temperature, network and disk usage. It starts the daemon if it is not running.
cliphist for the clipboard history ddcutil for brightness on external monitors without a backlight
cargo build --release packaging/stage.sh /tmp/stage Any Rust toolchain with edition 2024 works. stage.sh lays out usr/bin, the D-Bus service file and the licence.
Stop the daemon and run any command again to start a fresh one: taurus-core quit taurus-core sysinfo

Taurus ships its own blue light filter, taurus-gamma. It sets the color temperature, brightness, gamma and inversion of your displays on Wayland, with a day and night schedule that follows the sun. It is a small daemon, and the same binary is its command line client. They talk over the D-Bus session bus, so it needs no systemd. The binary links only glibc.

The taurus gamma command drives it, and starts it when needed. See the CLI reference. Taurus stops it on exit, and the compositor then restores normal colors. Without --output, a command changes every output, including outputs connected later.

The backend is picked on its own: Hyprland: its hyprland-ctm-control-v1 color matrix, when the compositor offers it. Hyprland no longer gives gamma ramps to clients. A matrix is linear, so only temperature and brightness take effect there. Gamma and inversion are accepted but have no effect. Sway, Niri, Mango, Umbriel and other wlroots-style compositors: the wlr-gamma-control-unstable-v1 protocol, where all four settings work. GNOME and KDE support neither. The colors last only while the daemon runs, since the compositor restores normal colors when a program's gamma control goes away. Gamma control is exclusive, so only one program can hold it per output. Stop any other night light tool first, or the compositor refuses the daemon's control and it logs a message.

taurus-gamma start # the daemon, in the background taurus-gamma set --temperature 4000 # every output taurus-gamma set -o eDP-1 --brightness 0.8 # one output taurus-gamma auto on --night 3500 # follow the schedule taurus-gamma location 55.75 37.62 # by the sun at this place taurus-gamma fallback 06:30 19:00 # or, without a location, by the clock taurus-gamma status -o eDP-1 taurus-gamma reset taurus-gamma quit # the compositor restores normal colors taurus-gamma --help lists every command. set takes --temperature K, --brightness 0-1, --gamma G and --inverted on|off. Setting a temperature turns the schedule off. reset returns to a neutral temperature, full brightness, gamma 1 and not inverted. status shows the color and the schedule, and fails if the daemon is not running. A command for an output that was just connected waits up to two seconds for it to appear. Commands never start the daemon themselves, except start.

The schedule changes the temperature with the time of day. It is off at start, and auto on turns it on. The daemon keeps no settings and finds no location itself: whatever starts it sets them, and they last until it exits. With a location, the temperature follows the sun's elevation: day at +2° and above, night at −4.5° and below, fading in between. That takes about 30 to 40 minutes at mid latitudes. Places without a sunrise or sunset, as in polar night, simply stay at night or day. Without a location, the fade to night starts at the fallback night time and the fade to day at the fallback day time, each lasting 30 minutes. They default to 19:00 and 07:00, and fallback DAY NIGHT changes them. The day and night temperatures default to 6500 K and 4000 K. auto on --day K --night K changes them. The fade is even in mireds (a million over the temperature), the scale on which equal steps look equally large. The schedule is applied every 10 seconds from the current clock, so suspend, time zone and daylight saving changes take effect at the next tick. Brightness, gamma and inversion are left alone by the schedule.

The color for each temperature is computed from physics, not a curve fit: Planck's law gives the blackbody spectrum. The CIE 1931 color matching functions turn it into XYZ. A Bradford chromatic adaptation maps the 6500 K blackbody onto the display's D65 white, so 6500 K is exactly neutral and the colors change smoothly around it. The sRGB transfer function encodes the result, because a gamma ramp scales encoded values. The sun's position comes from NOAA's equations and agrees with PyEphem to about 0.01°.

The daemon owns org.taurus.Gamma on the session bus. Object / controls every output, and /outputs/<name> controls one. Output names become path elements with every character other than a letter or digit replaced by _, so eDP-1 is /outputs/eDP_1. busctl --user set-property org.taurus.Gamma / org.taurus.Gamma Temperature q 4000 busctl --user set-property org.taurus.Gamma /outputs/eDP_1 org.taurus.Gamma Brightness d 0.8 busctl --user call org.taurus.Gamma / org.taurus.Gamma ToggleInverted busctl --user tree org.taurus.Gamma Member Type Range Temperature property q 1000 to 10000 K, 6500 is neutral Brightness property d 0 to 1 Gamma property d at least 0.1, 1 is neutral Inverted property b UpdateTemperature method n adds a delta UpdateBrightness, UpdateGamma method d adds a delta ToggleInverted method The schedule lives on the org.taurus.Gamma.Schedule interface, with Auto, DayTemperature, NightTemperature, SetLocation, ClearLocation, the fallback times and read-only values for the sun. Reading / gives the average of all outputs, and writing to / changes every output, including outputs connected later. All properties emit PropertiesChanged. The full list of members is in the taurus-gamma README.

The install script downloads the latest release for x86_64, checks it against the published checksums and installs it to /usr/local/bin. On other architectures it prints a warning and leaves the shell without the blue light filter, so build it from source there. Running the installer again updates it, and it does nothing when the installed version is already the latest. The Arch packages bundle a release, and the Nix flake builds it from source.
taurus-gamma --version taurus-gamma start taurus-gamma set --temperature 4000 taurus-gamma reset The screen should turn warmer and then return to normal. If it doesn't, see below.

The package installs share/dbus-1/services/org.taurus.Gamma.service, so the first call to org.taurus.Gamma starts the daemon. A process D-Bus starts gets D-Bus's own environment, so WAYLAND_DISPLAY must be in it. Most compositor setups already run dbus-update-activation-environment --systemd WAYLAND_DISPLAY. If yours doesn't, start the daemon from the compositor's autostart instead. The shell does this for you with taurus gamma start.

GNOME and KDE are not supported. Another night light tool may hold the gamma control. Gamma control is exclusive per output, so stop the other tool first. Hyprland only applies temperature and brightness.
cargo build --release packaging/stage.sh /tmp/stage Any Rust toolchain with edition 2024 works. stage.sh lays out usr/bin, the D-Bus service file and the licence.

IMPORTANT Migrating from v1: All previous configuration will be backed up and unused. Configuration of compositor settings such as monitors, keybinds, and autostart is now up to you, as the project migrated from being dotfiles to being a shell. Taurus installs on Arch Linux and its derivatives (pacman, with systemd or OpenRC). Other distributions are not supported for now. Use this installer: curl -fsSL https://0x0ar.github.io/taurus/install.sh | bash If this doesn't work, use: bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0x0ar/taurus/main/install/install.sh)" NOTE To update, run the installer script again and choose Update. In the installer's configuration list, Default browser lets you pick Firefox, Chromium, Brave, or Zen. The installer adds the matching package, sets it as the system default browser, and points the Mod+F compositor bind at it. Your choice is saved for later updates.

Arch Linux and its derivatives (EndeavourOS, Manjaro, CachyOS, Garuda, Artix and others) are supported on systemd, OpenRC and other init systems. Umbriel is installed from the AUR package umbriel-git, so an AUR helper is required; the installer sets up yay if none is present.

Arch-based distributions can build Taurus as a native package from this repository instead of running the installer script. The package installs the shell system-wide and pulls in every runtime dependency the installer would. The parts of the installer that change your home directory, services, or login screen are not done by a package, so you run them yourself afterwards. The repository contains two PKGBUILDs in packaging/aur, and they conflict with each other: Package Builds taurus The latest tagged release taurus-git The latest commit on main Install the build tools: sudo pacman -S --needed base-devel git Then clone the repository and build the package: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/0x0ar/taurus.git cd taurus/packaging/aur/taurus makepkg -si For the latest commit instead of the latest release, use cd taurus/packaging/aur/taurus-git. makepkg -si installs the remaining dependencies with pacman, builds the package, and installs it. IMPORTANT Do not run the installer script on a system where Taurus is installed this way. It would place a second copy in ~/.local/share/taurus and link it over the packaged one. Update by rebuilding the package, as described below, and use the steps that follow for anything the installer would otherwise do. If the in-app update notification offers to run the installer, ignore it.

Installer step Package Install dependencies Done, including Iosevka Nerd Font Replace quickshell-git with quickshell Done, the package conflicts with quickshell-git and installs quickshell Install taurus and taurusd Done, in /usr/bin Install taurus-audio Done, taurus-audio in /usr/bin Install taurus-gamma Done, taurus-gamma in /usr/bin Install taurus-core Done, taurus-core in /usr/bin Lock screen PAM service Done, /etc/pam.d/taurus SDDM theme files Done, in /usr/share/sddm/themes/material-you Compositor configs Manual, step 1 Kitty, Cava, and Fastfetch configs Manual, step 2 Wallpapers Manual, step 3 Taurus settings Manual, step 4 System services Manual, step 5 Qt icon theme Manual, step 6 SDDM configuration Manual and optional, step 7 First launch guide Manual, step 8 The installer's anonymous install telemetry has no equivalent, so a package install sends none.

The packaged files live in /usr/share/taurus. These steps copy what you need into your home directory and are written to be pasted into a shell one after another, since later steps reuse variables from earlier ones. share=/usr/share/taurus cfg="${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}" 1. Compositor config​ Install the compositors you want, for example sudo pacman -S hyprland. The package lists Hyprland, Niri, Sway, Mango, and Umbriel as optional dependencies. Then copy the matching config. Choose one row: Compositor comp dir Hyprland hyprland hypr Niri niri niri Sway sway sway Mango mango mango Umbriel umbriel umbriel comp=hyprland dir=hypr if [ -d "$cfg/$dir" ]; then backup="$cfg/${dir}_backup/backup_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)" mkdir -p "$backup" cp -a "$cfg/$dir/." "$backup/" fi mkdir -p "$cfg/$dir" cp -r "$share/compositors/$comp/." "$cfg/$dir/" Your existing config is backed up first. Files with the same name in the new config replace yours, so move any personal settings back from the backup afterwards. 2. Kitty, Cava, and Fastfetch configs​ for app in kitty cava fastfetch; do mkdir -p "$cfg/$app" cp -r "$share/config/$app/." "$cfg/$app/" done This replaces files with the same name. Skip any app whose config you want to keep. 3. Wallpapers​ pictures="$(xdg-user-dir PICTURES 2>/dev/null)" if [ -z "$pictures" ] || [ "$pictures" = "$HOME" ]; then pictures="$HOME/Pictures" fi wallpapers="$pictures/Wallpapers" repo="${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/taurus-wallpapers" mkdir -p "$wallpapers" git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/ilyamiro/shell-wallpapers.git "$repo" find "$repo" -path "$repo/.git" -prune -o -type f \ \( -iname '*.jpg' -o -iname '*.jpeg' -o -iname '*.png' -o -iname '*.gif' -o -iname '*.webp' \) \ -exec cp -t "$wallpapers" {} + This is the full wallpaper pack. To keep only a few, copy those files out of $repo instead of running the last command. 4. Taurus settings​ This merges the default settings with any settings you already have, keeps your values, and points the shell at your wallpaper folder: settings="$cfg/taurus/settings.json" mkdir -p "$cfg/taurus" [ -s "$settings" ] || echo '{}' > "$settings" jq -s --arg wp "$wallpapers" '(.[0] * .[1]) * {wallpaperDir: $wp}' \ "$share/config/taurus/settings.json" "$settings" > "$settings.tmp" \ && mv "$settings.tmp" "$settings" bash "$share/src/scripts/location.sh" --refresh The last command detects your location for the weather widget. Skip it if you prefer to set the location by hand. 5. Services​ On systemd, enable the audio stack, networking, and power profiles: sudo systemctl --global enable pipewire wireplumber pipewire-pulse systemctl --user enable --now pipewire wireplumber pipewire-pulse sudo systemctl enable --now NetworkManager power-profiles-daemon On OpenRC, dinit, runit, or s6, enable NetworkManager and power-profiles-daemon with your init system's tools, and make sure PipeWire and WirePlumber start with your session. 6. Qt icon theme​ for qt in qt6ct; do mkdir -p "$cfg/$qt" [ -f "$cfg/$qt/$qt.conf" ] || printf '[Appearance]
icon_theme=Adwaita
' > "$cfg/$qt/$qt.conf" done if [ -z "$QT_QPA_PLATFORMTHEME" ] && ! grep -rqs '^QT_QPA_PLATFORMTHEME=' "$cfg/environment.d"; then mkdir -p "$cfg/environment.d" printf 'QT_QPA_PLATFORMTHEME=qt6ct
' > "$cfg/environment.d/taurus-qt.conf" fi If you already have a qt6ct.conf, set icon_theme=Adwaita under [Appearance] yourself. Log out and back in for the environment variable to apply. 7. SDDM login screen (optional)​ The theme files are already installed. Install SDDM and its Qt dependencies, then configure it: sudo pacman -S --needed sddm qt6-declarative qt6-svg [ -f /etc/sddm.conf ] && sudo mv /etc/sddm.conf "/etc/sddm.conf.backup.$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)" sudo mkdir -p /etc/sddm.conf.d sudo tee /etc/sddm.conf.d/10-material-you.conf > /dev/null <<'CONF' [Theme] Current=material-you ThemeDir=/usr/share/sddm/themes [General] InputMethod= CONF /etc/sddm.conf overrides the files in /etc/sddm.conf.d, so it is moved aside. To run the greeter on Wayland, add these two lines under [General]: DisplayServer=wayland GreeterEnvironment=QT_WAYLAND_DISABLE_WINDOWDECORATION=1 If another display manager is enabled, disable it before enabling SDDM, for example sudo systemctl disable gdm. Then enable SDDM: sudo systemctl enable sddm.service 8. First launch​ Show the welcome guide on the next start: rm -f "${XDG_STATE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/state}/taurus/first_launch.done" Log in to your compositor. The configs from step 1 start Taurus on login. If you kept your own compositor config, add taurusd start to its autostart.

Set TAURUS_EXTRAS to a space-separated list before running the installer: TAURUS_EXTRAS="tmux openrgb" bash install/install.sh tmux: installs tmux and an Omarchy-style ~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf (an existing file is kept as tmux.conf.taurus-backup). openrgb: installs OpenRGB, a rgb-off.service that turns all lighting off at boot. The RGB tab of the settings window (Mod+H) needs OpenRGB.

To update, pull the repository and build again. The new package replaces the installed one: cd taurus git pull cd packaging/aur/taurus makepkg -si Removing the package leaves everything in your home directory alone: sudo pacman -Rns taurus Delete ~/.config/taurus, ~/.local/state/taurus, and ~/.cache/taurus yourself if you also want your settings gone.
